title: The last words
hook: "decay is inherent in all component things; work out your salvation with diligence" (DN 16, Rhys Davids)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Subhadda, turned away three times and called in by the Buddha. Your line: there's still time.

What would you say, if you knew they were your last words? Some famous last words are funny, some are grand, and some were polished by whoever wrote them down. It's deep in the night at Kusinara, between the sal trees. The monks are gathered around. Ananda is there. Subhadda has been ordained. And the Buddha has a few things left to say. First, practical things. When I'm gone, he tells Ananda, don't think you have no teacher. The teaching and the discipline I've given you will be your teacher. Then he asks the monks, three times, if anyone has any doubt left about the teaching. Ask now, so you won't regret it. Nobody speaks.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOUR LAST WORDS BE?` → `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.` → `ANY DOUBT? ASK NOW.`

segments.voice: Then come the last words. In the 1881 translation by T. W. Rhys Davids: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Everything put together comes apart, so keep going, with care. The Pali word at the heart of it is appamada: heedfulness, carefulness, not letting yourself drift. A modern rendering puts it: strive on with diligence. Not a dramatic promise. Not a claim about himself. The same two things he had taught all along, compressed into one breath: things end, so practice. Then he passes through the stages of deep meditation, up and back down and up again, and from the fourth, the text says, he passes away. Today's word names that: parinibbana, complete nibbana, the full going-out of an awakened one at death. Buddhist traditions understand that ending in more than one way, and the Buddha himself refused to describe it in ordinary terms of existing or not existing. The earth trembles. Ananda speaks a short, shaken verse. In Theravada countries, the festival of Vesak remembers this night together with the birth and the awakening, on one full-moon day. Look back at this week of last days. The old cart that still rolled. Be your own island. Vesali, lovely, and the elephant look. Cunda's meal, and no one to blame. Rest at Kusinara. Subhadda, and still time. And today, the last words. The whole life comes down to a line you could carry in your pocket.
screen: `DECAY IS INHERENT IN ALL THINGS.` · `APPAMADA: CAREFUL, NOT DRIFTING.` · `PARINIBBANA, THE FULL GOING-OUT.` · `A WEEK OF LAST DAYS.` · then, large: `STRIVE ON WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: Sit in silence, with no instruction except the last one he gave. Let everything that arises in you arise, and everything that passes, pass; if your mind drifts, come back, gently, with care. Things end. Keep going.
Parinibbana. Complete nibbana: the final passing of an awakened one, at Kusinara, after the last words.
Your line: strive on with care. His whole teaching, in one breath. Day eighty-four, complete.

screen: `DAY 84 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HARE IN THE MOON.`

howItsDone: In Theravada countries Vesak remembers the parinibbana together with the birth and awakening, East Asian traditions keep Nirvana Day, and the last words on heedfulness are often recited and quoted.

original.note: Pali: complete nibbana, the final passing of an awakened one. Sanskrit parinirvāṇa.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha died.
what it means: parinibbana, the complete going-out of an awakened one, after last words about impermanence and care.
what a scholar hears: DN 16, 6.7: vayadhamma sankhara, appamadena sampadetha; the Buddha declined to describe the one who has gone beyond in terms of existing or not existing.
recall: birth; here, his new life as a monk

notes: Rhys Davids 1881 (SBE XI, The Book of the Great Decease, ch. 6 §10) quoted: 'Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!' Please check punctuation against the SBE text.
Outline's practice says 'three minutes'; the app's sit is two minutes, so the practice is written for two.

Parinibbana understood differently across schools; the script says so and notes the Buddha's refusal to describe the tathagata after death as existing or not (the unanswered questions, e.g. MN 72). Confirm framing.
Vesak (Theravada) and Nirvana Day (East Asian, Feb 15) mentioned in howItsDone. Confirm.
